Abeyance

uh-BAY-ins -- from Old French abeance ('gaping, expectation'); almost always used in 'in abeyance.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Abeyance is a state of temporary suspension or inactivity.

With both co-founders out on medical leave, the merger talks were placed in abeyance until fall.

Worked Example

The historic downtown mural project was held in abeyance for two years while the city searched for enough funding to finish it properly.

The project wasn't cancelled -- it was paused, with every intention of picking it back up once the money showed up. That temporary, on-hold status is exactly what abeyance describes.

How Abeyance Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

dormancy

dormancy: a state of being temporarily inactive

suspension

suspension: an official, formal halt to something

Antonyms

activation

activation: the act of setting something into motion

enforcement

enforcement: making sure a rule is actively carried out

How Strong Is It? — dormancy → abeyance → suspension

dormancy vs. abeyance

dormancy vs. abeyance: Dormancy is gentler than abeyance: a dormant volcano simply rests on its own, while holding a plan in abeyance is a firmer, deliberate act of setting it aside.

suspension vs. abeyance

suspension vs. abeyance: Suspension is stronger than abeyance: a rule held in abeyance quietly waits unused, but a referee's suspension of a game is an active, official halt to everything.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Abeyance came into English from Old French abeance, 'a gaping in expectation,' and its root never produced other common English words. So the word is best learned whole: something in abeyance is left open and waiting -- paused rather than resolved.

Use the root in a new word: abeyant

Use the root in a new word: abeyant: The estate's abeyant title passed through three generations before any single heir could formally claim it.

Word Building

Word Choice

Abeyance almost always appears in the fixed phrase 'in abeyance' -- a formal, businesslike way to say something has been paused with the clear expectation of picking it back up later, not cancelled for good.
